chunks: Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) passed by me while I was seated in the presence of a judge in Al-Medina. So I went to him the next morning, and he said to me: 'What was that gathering I saw you in yesterday?' He said: I replied to him, 'May I be your ransom! This judge is generous towards me, so I sometimes sit with him.' So he said to me: 'And what would secure you from the Curse descending and encompassing everyone in the gathering?'

key_terms.اللَّعْنَة: Divine curse or condemnation; in Islamic theology, la'nah is the removal of divine mercy and can descend upon individuals or groups engaged in sin
key_terms.الْقَاضِي: Judge; in classical Islamic jurisprudence, a qadi was appointed by the ruling authority to adjudicate disputes according to Islamic law
key_terms.الْمَجْلِس: The gathering or assembly; here refers specifically to the court session of the judge
key_terms.جُعِلْتُ فِدَاكَ: A Shia devotional formula of reverence: 'May I be sacrificed for you' — expressing deep respect toward the Imam

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Baqir or al-Sadiq say about sitting with unjust judges?
ai.summary: Muhammad ibn Muslim, one of the closest companions of the Imams, narrates how Imam al-Baqir or Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon them) sternly rebuked him for sitting in the company of an unjust judge in Medina, even though the narrator's reason was merely social — the judge was personally generous to him. The Imam's rebuke carries a warning about the spiritual danger of proximity to oppressive authority: divine curse does not discriminate based on personal relationships, but can descend upon entire gatherings. This teaching reflects the Shia ethical principle that one must actively dissociate from unjust rulers and their courts.
